raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old Sri Lankan Tamil male, was presented to a tertiary care hospital in Northern Province of Sri Lanka with a history of high-grade fever of 3-days duration which was associated with myalgia, arthralgia and retro-orbital pain. He also had vomiting and loss of appetite for preceding 3 days. He never experienced an abdominal pain or distention. He had no mucocutaneous bleeding manifestations on presentation. He had no symptoms suggestive of either respiratory or urinary tract infection. There was no past medical history of note. He is an ethanol user, consuming 16 units per week for last 10 years. He did admit a history of binge drinking during the initial course of the illness to relieve his pain.
On arrival, he was conscious and rational. He was febrile with a temperature of 38.6 C. He was not pale or icteric. His capillary refilling time was less than 2 s. There were no peripheral lymphadenopathy, petechial rashes, ecchymotic patches or stigmata of chronic liver disease.
His pulse rate was 84 beats/min and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg without a significant postural drop. There was no clinical evidence of pleural effusion or free fluid in the abdomen. Abdomen was soft, non-tender, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. There were no features of neurological deficit or meningeal irritation. Rest of the clinical examination was unremarkable including the optic fundus.
Initial full blood count showed white blood cells (WBCs) of 3.91 x 109cells/L with neutrophil 3.22 x 109/L and lymphocytes 0.37 x 109/L. Hemoglobin, hematocrit and platelet were 16.1 g/dL, 46.1% and 142 x 109/L, respectively. Initial liver biochemistry showed alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 3760 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 9352 U/L. Prothrombin time was 16.3 s (standard: 10-13 s). Renal function and urine full report were normal. The dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen in serum became positive on day 3 of illness (day of admission).
He was managed in the ward during the initial 48 h with usual supportive care in addition to the standard fluid therapy according to the national dengue management protocol. During this 48 h, the clinical parameters remained within the normal limits.
Although he had defervescence on day 5, he became restless. His conscious state, pulse rate blood pressure and capillary blood glucose were normal, and there was no postural drop or bleeding manifestations. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Full blood count showed WBC 4.17 x 109cells/L (neutrophil 64%, lymphocytes 30%), hemoglobin 17.6 g/dL, hematocrit 46.8% and platelet count 27 x 109cells/L. Liver biochemistry was as follows: ALT of 8648 U/L, AST of 28,373 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 155 U/L (range: 46-116), albumin 37 g/L and total bilirubin 55.1 mumol/L with direct bilirubin 30 mumol/L. Prothrombin time was elevated to 21.3 s. His other routine biochemical investigations such as blood glucose, renal function tests, serum calcium and venous blood gas were within normal range. A bed side ultrasound scan did not reveal any evidence of plasma leakage.
On the same day night, ceiling of medical care was escalated and patient was transferred to High Dependency Unit. At this point of care, he was diagnosed with acute liver failure with grade III hepatic encephalopathy evidence by deranged liver biochemistry, coagulopathy and altered level of sensorium, and he was started on intravenous NAC infusion (150 mg/kg in 250 mL of 5% dextrose over 15 min, then 50 mg/kg in 500 mL 5% dextrose over 4 h followed by 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL of 5% dextrose over 16 h). Furthermore, he also received lactulose and metronidazole as a part of the treatment for hepatic encephalopathy. Throughout the course of illness, he had never experienced a shock and his vitals were stable except the altered level of consciousness. He was never given supra-therapeutic dose of paracetamol, any other medicines, herbals or traditional medicines that could cause liver injury. He had no clinical, laboratory or radiology evidence of plasma leakage throughout the course of illness. Furthermore, he also developed features of alcohol withdrawal and it was managed with intravenous thiamine and short acting benzodiazepines.
With the above treatment, his cognitive state started to improve. AST and ALT started to decline gradually from the day 6 of the illness as shown in Table 1. On day 7 of illness, the dengue serology (both immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM)) was positive. Even though co-existence of alcoholic hepatitis was considered, however, it does not explain the degree of elevation of transaminases in this patient. Since the clinical scenario and the serological evidence confirmed a dengue infection, we did not explore for an alternate cause of hepatic injury other than the work up for co-infections with primary hepatitis virus A, B and C which all became negative. On day 15, patient was sent home after complete recovery.
On review a month later, he was asymptomatic and had successfully abstained from alcohol. His follow-up liver profile and ultrasound scan of the abdomen showed no abnormalities except mild fatty liver.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever, myalgia, arthralgia, retro-orbital pain, vomiting, and loss of appetite for three days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 34-year-old male presented with a 3-day history of high-grade fever associated with myalgia, arthralgia, retro-orbital pain, vomiting, and anorexia. He received supportive care and intravenous fluid therapy. On day 5 of illness following defervescence, he became acutely restless and developed right upper quadrant tenderness with severe hepatic encephalopathy (grade III) and coagulopathy, necessitating transfer to the High Dependency Unit. Throughout admission, he had no episodes of shock or evidence of plasma leakage.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant medical history. Alcohol consumption of 16 units per week for 10 years, with a history of binge drinking during the initial course of illness to relieve pain. No history of supratherapeutic paracetamol, herbal medicines, or traditional remedies.
subjective.review_of_systems: Loss of appetite, vomiting; denies abdominal pain or distension on presentation, mucocutaneous bleeding, respiratory symptoms, or urinary tract symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Conscious and rational. Temperature 38.6 °C, pulse rate 84 beats/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg without postural drop, capillary refill time < 2 seconds. No pallor, icterus, peripheral lymphadenopathy, petechiae, ecchymoses, or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Abdomen soft, non-tender, without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Respiratory examination normal; no pleural effusion. Neurological examination unremarkable with normal optic fundi. Day 5 (HDU transfer): Restless, altered level of consciousness (grade III hepatic encephalopathy), mild right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness, vitals stable without postural drop or bleeding.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 3 (admission): WBC 3.91 x 10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 3.22 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.37 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin 16.1 g/dL, hematocrit 46.1%, platelet count 142 x 10^9/L; ALT 3,760 U/L, AST 9,352 U/L, prothrombin time 16.3 seconds (standard: 10-13 seconds); renal function and urinalysis normal. Day 5: WBC 4.17 x 10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 30%), hemoglobin 17.6 g/dL, hematocrit 46.8%, platelet count 27 x 10^9/L; ALT 8,648 U/L, AST 28,373 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 155 U/L (reference: 46-116 U/L), albumin 37 g/L, total bilirubin 55.1 micromol/L, direct bilirubin 30 micromol/L, prothrombin time 21.3 seconds; blood glucose, renal function tests, serum calcium, and venous blood gas normal. Bedside ultrasound: No evidence of plasma leakage, ascites, or pleural effusion; repeat ultrasound at 1 month showed mild fatty liver. Viral serologies: Acute hepatitis A, B, and C negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Dengue virus infection (expanded dengue syndrome) manifested by acute liver failure with massive transaminitis (AST > 28,000 U/L, ALT > 8,000 U/L), grade III hepatic encephalopathy, and coagulopathy in the absence of plasma leakage or shock, complicated by concurrent alcohol withdrawal. Confirmed by positive serum Dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen on day 3 of illness and positive Dengue serology (IgM and IgG) on day 7. Viral hepatitis A, B, and C, acetaminophen toxicity, and alternative causes of acute liver injury were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Transferred to High Dependency Unit. Managed with standard intravenous fluid resuscitation, intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) infusion protocol (150 mg/kg in 250 mL 5% dextrose over 15 min, then 50 mg/kg in 500 mL over 4 h, followed by 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL over 16 h), lactulose, and metronidazole for hepatic encephalopathy. Alcohol withdrawal managed with intravenous thiamine and short-acting benzodiazepines. The patient showed gradual neurological and biochemical recovery, transaminases steadily declined, and he was discharged on day 15. At 1-month follow-up, he remained completely asymptomatic with normalized liver enzymes and sustained alcohol abstinence.
